utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good afternoon. This is Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before we start, I was informed that you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, would like to address the Chamber briefly. I suggest that we do that after the examination of Witness DP6. And before we start with the examination of Witness DP6, I perhaps owe an explanation to everyone in and around this courtroom. Being confronted yesterday at the very end of the morning session with a request of the Prosecution, I indicated that the Chamber would try to find out whether Witness DP6 was still available and what the merits were of the request. We did that quickly. We found out that Witness DP6 was scheduled to leave this morning, and, therefore, the Chamber gave it a great effort to see whether DP6 could be additionally cross-examined yesterday afternoon by the Prosecution. That caused everyone to stand by -- and, General Galic, that includes you. I know that you have been transported from the detention facility to the building of the Tribunal -- this was all done in order to see whether we could save time and whether we could allow the witness of which we all know that he has been waiting for quite a considerable time, and that he testified for a couple of days in this court, whether we could allow him to leave this morning. Finally, not everyone could be reached. And since it is impossible to examine a witness in the absence of Defence counsel, finally we had to establish that what we tried to do was not possible yesterday in the afternoon. I apologise -- well, at least I regret that all those who were standby, who were here in this courtroom -- of course, the Judges even, although not in this courtroom, were also standby in order to see whether we could achieve what we intended to do. We highly regret that you were here, finally, for nothing. I would like to explain this to everyone before we start with the examination of Witness DP6. The Prosecution, the Chamber has decided that it gives the Prosecution an opportunity to put further questions in cross-examination to Witness DP6. Since the summary of the testimony of Witness DP4 did not indicate a -- an issue on which the Defence specifically asked the witness about an issue that -- an issue that could have played a role in the zone of responsibility as we heard his testimony of Witness DP6, and, therefore, the Prosecution is allowed to put additional questions to Witness DP6. I take it that Mr. Usher is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that the Prosecution understands that questions are allowed in respect of this issue. Yes. The usher left the courtroom, so I take it that he is trying to escort DP6 into the courtroom. In respect of Witness DP6, facial distortion is in effect as a protective measure and a pseudonym. So if facial distortion is effective at this very moment, the witness could be brought in. Could I get a confirmation from the technical booth that facial distortion is effective. It is. Please, Mr. Usher, escort Mr. DP6 into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Good afternoon. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...I will shortly explain to you that a few questions might be put to you, although you concluded your testimony before. It is for procedural reasons that the Chamber has decided that the Prosecution is allowed to put additional questions to you. We tried to do everything, as you may have noticed, to continue your examination yesterday in the afternoon so that you could leave as it was scheduled this morning. Unfortunately, we could not proceed. We very much wished to do so, but we finally could not since Defence counsel were not available at that time. That is the reason why we had to ask you to leave one day later. We really very much regret that we had to ask this to you. Mr. Ierace, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. President, just before my learned colleague speaks, to save time, could the Registrar please obtain ready to give to the witness Exhibit D1760. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, one thing chronologically so as to make things clear. I will speak later, but we think that the rights of the Defence are breached with this delay, but I will speak on this later on. We shall participate in this, but we wish to indicate this clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, could you already start or do you need the exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I think I can start, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sir, you told us on the 16th of October that you did not personally have any contact with UNPROFOR representatives. Do you remember giving that evidence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't have any contact with the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You were asked whether in your locality and during the conflict there were any UNPROFOR forces there, and you said that they came to the student hostels from time to time. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You added that they went to the student hostels from time to time in August or September. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1992, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You did not give a year and that was my next question. I take it that was 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness speak up, please. We could not hear his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The interpreters can not hear you. Could you please speak a bit more in the microphone, Mr. DP6. Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you answer yes to that question? I think I heard you say "Da."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, you also gave some evidence about the old people's home. You indicated its position on a photograph, and you also indicated that it was on your portion of the front line, that is, the portion of the front line which was the responsibility of the company that you commanded. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You told us on the 16th of October that the old people's home was shelled in June, perhaps between 15th and 20th of June, you couldn't recall the date exactly. Do you remember giving that evidence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Was that June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And you said that the same thing happened in July, another shell hit the old people's home. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say it was in July -- that in July a shell fell. Shells were falling until July. And in July, I remember it well, that the old people were killed from infantry weapons in July. The first shell hit the old people's home in mid-June, and six old people were killed on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, and I think your words were, "and the same thing happened in July, there was another shell that hit the old people's home." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was one in July. But I think I said that -- I mean, in July also a few old people were killed from infantry weapons. But shells were falling. But the first one hit the old people's home in mid-June 1992, the first shell. I know that very well, although I cannot remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Whenever the exact dates were, I take it you are referring to June and July of 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, on the 10th of September 1992 at 12.00 mid-day, was that home evacuated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The old people's home was never evacuated -- I mean in Nedzarici. The old people in Nedzarici was there functioning until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Are you telling us that old people continued to live in that building throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The home on the front line; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was right behind the Centre for the Blind. It wasn't on the front line, but some 60, 70 metres away from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sir, why did that happen? Given that the building was shelled --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I object to the question. The question doesn't make sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I haven't finished the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is it, why was it -- why did that happen? It doesn't make sense; the fact that old people were there for the duration of the war. I think that Mr. Ierace should make more precise the wording of his question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, as I have already indicated twice, I haven't finished asking the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Why did that happen? Given that it was shelled with resulting casualties in June and July of 1992, why was it not evacuated?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I object to the question. I object to it because in line with Rules, Mr. Ierace should first check whether this witness can know such a thing, if there was manager of this. Otherwise, it invites a hypothetical answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. DP6, do you know why the inhabitants of the elderly people's home were not evacuated after the building was shelled? Do you know it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know why and what for. All I know is that they were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No one ever told you why they were not evacuated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that in the early days of the war, the Jews left for Belgrade. That is what I heard from Milena who worked there. Perhaps it was after the war that I heard it. She worked in the old people's home and she was the manager. But why these people were not evacuated, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Were they living in the basement of the building during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were living on the ground floor, the first floor. Those old people who had stayed there. Before the war they were about -- I don't know really -- some 250, 300. But as the time went by, naturally old men, people died, people died of old age, some were killed, so the number declined steadily. And they were living there. And truth to tell, I didn't go into their rooms. All I know is that they usually spent their time on the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: By the time you were wounded in February of 1993, how many civilian old people were there living in that building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why, I don't know. I couldn't give you the number. There must have been around 150 or plus/minus. I don't really know the exact number. I wasn't really interested to know, so I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Why were you not interested to know, given that you were the commander of the company that had control of that part of the front line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't try that because Mrs. Milena - and she was the director of the old people's home - she was the one who looked after them. Only if somebody was wounded and killed and had to be taken out, then she would ask us to help her. And we always were there to come -- to lend her a hand to get those people out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that the -- General Galic, that you want to address us, but is there any technical problem?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. I merely wanted to talk to my counsel, if I may. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ierace, before I ask you to proceed, we have heard a lot of questions now. I can't imagine that these were introductory questions to the issue for which you asked specifically to re-examine the witness. Could you come to your point because we heard a lot about the building now, but not on the specific issue you raised in your request.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: There are two aspects in turn to this particular aspect, Mr. President, having regard to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was asking something to Mr. Ierace, and I will ask him to respond, unless you would like to say that the witness should take his earphones off at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly. Exactly. I think we should apply the same procedure, that the witness be asked to remove his headsets. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you take off your headsets. Mr. Ierace, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. In the interest of saving time, I will just continue with the questioning. I obviously accept what you have said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. Could you -- thank you, Mr. DP6.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: At any stage when you were in command of the forces covering that building, did you utilise any part of the building for military purposes?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this type of question could have been -- could have been asked very well during the regular examination of this witness. This is really, really, really not acceptable at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, we just invited you to come to your point. Again, if this would be the final introductory question, we will allow you, but then please come to the issue you raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I think that the answer the witness gave to the question was "no."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that correct, Mr. DP6? You said that the building was never used for military purposes. I didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did say that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: At any stage, was the building used as an observation post by the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The United Nations came from time to time and used that old people's home as an observation point. I know they went up to the upper floor. I didn't -- upper floors. I didn't -- I did not see them, but I saw their vehicles in front of the old people's home.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: So, therefore, what you saw were UN vehicles in front of the old people's home, even though you never saw the UN individuals themselves. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did see these people, but they went upstairs to the upper floors of the old people's home and they were probably observing, they were checking something. I don't know because I was not with them. Only when they would come to the old people's home, they weren't shooting at -- in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Whereabouts did you see them? Did you see them going into the building, leaving the building, for instance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw them come in; I saw them come out.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And is that all you saw of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's all I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you receive any information from your superiors as to whether they should be permitted to have access to that part of the front line that you commanded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From the command of the battalion, we would hear the -- UNPROFOR would come to the old people's home, that they would be there, spend some time and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: How much notice did you receive of their arrival from your battalion commander? In other words, how long before they arrived were you notified?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, maybe just before they would come, the commander of the battalion would let us know maybe an hour to an hour and a half before their arrival. I don't remember any more. But probably as they were approaching the command post. I don't really know, but this is when they would let us know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Given that you only saw them enter the building and retreat from the building, you do not know from your own observations what they did in the building. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you mean you don't know what they did in the building; is that what you are saying? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Of course, yeah, yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, to your knowledge, was there an observation post operated by UNPROFOR in Nedzarici in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know if there was observation posts. But I know that it would come from time to time to the old people's home, and they would observe whatever they were observing. I really don't know what is it they were doing there. But to tell you there was a special post, I really couldn't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Did you have any contact with [redacted]between September, the beginning of September 1992 and February 1993 when you were wounded? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not see the pertinence in this question with regards to the issue that the accusations should limit itself. I do not see why one is asking questions about observation posts held by the UN. And I don't even remember, I don't even know myself, who is [redacted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, I ask the witness to take off his headphones.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, I am happy to assist my learned colleague. He will find in response to his statement just made that he doesn't even know himself who is [redacted], but if he looks under his filing of Rule 65 ter, he will see that he is Defence witness number 36.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But, Mr. President, I would really like to be understood correctly. I do not know what this [redacted], and I am extremely grateful to the accusation of reminding me of this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, first of all, may I ask -- have protective measures have been granted in respect of the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could then a redaction be made as to the -- on from where the name for the first time appears. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if the Prosecution knows who this person is, if the Defence knows who this person is, and if the witness doesn't say, "what are you talking about," then it is not necessary to ask anything else. It seems, as far as I understand, clear that the Defence knows what person the Prosecution refers to and it seems that the witness knows. So, therefore, I think there is no reason to ask Mr. Ierace to explain that. But we were still listening to Mr. Ierace explaining the relevance of his questions in respect of this person of which the name just has been redacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, would you like me to give that explanation now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In material disclosed to the Defence is a diary of [redacted] who was a senior subordinate in the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. An entry in that diary for the 10th of September, 1992, reads in part, "evacuation of old people's home at 1200 hours." Mr. President, that concludes my questions, although I would be grateful if the -- I do press that question and the answer given by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did the witness answer the question, as a matter of fact?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. He answered, "no."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He answered no. Then if that concludes your questions. Then, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, as usual, if there are any questions that came up as a result from the cross-examination --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, what line of questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are some.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Witness, could you please put your headphones on again. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, you explained to us that you were examined in length about the old people's home. What can you tell us with what you know with regards to the way people lived at the time, that is to say, during the war? For instance, were they obliged to hide, to protect themselves from shots, from --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will withdraw my examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object to the question anyway, Mr. President. That doesn't arise out of cross-examination. The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would say that you have put questions to the witness in respect of where the people who inhabited the building lived, and I think that is an issue, a specific issue. So the objection is denied. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell this Chamber, please, if you know, how did these people lived at the time, these elderly, and if you can give us some details, we would appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the old people's home, in 1992, as I said earlier, there were approximately 250 to 300 elderly. I don't know any more. I know this because Mrs. Milena related this to me, some of the Jews had left, and other people who could go somewhere, they left. So they were left with 150 people, from 100 to 150 elderly. So I know that during the first year of the war in 1992, these elderly who were mobile would go through Nedzarici, they would leave the home, and they would try to get some water from the well. And they would go to the gardens of the people who had some gardens, the inhabitants of the area, and I know that they would receive some food and vegetables from the people. And also the army -- whenever the army would distribute food to us, meals, they would come to distribute meals to us, we would also share our meals with the elderly. We would give them one-third of our meals so they would have something to eat. And this was up until the time where Mrs. Milena -- I think that it was at the end of 1992, early 1993, somebody from the UNPROFOR came. And I know that that's when the first humanitarian aid started arriving. And it was a bit easier for them to survive that way. So those who were mobile, the elderly who could move around walk about up until the time the humanitarian aid started arriving, they would gather some vegetables, they would go and come back. And I know they were receiving something from the Ilijas municipality and also there was a priest, I think his name was Momo, he was also helping.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. No more questions regarding these old people's home, Witness. You told us that the elderly belonging to the ethnicity or the culture -- I don't even know how to call it anymore -- but who were Jewish, Jewish ethnicity, that they had left. Now, I would like to ask you the following questions: Which are the ethnicities that left? People belonging to which ethnicities remained in the home after the departure of the Jews?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were all types of ethnicity Muslim, Serbs, and Croats. But I would like to add this: In that old people's home, there was a woman called Ramiza, she worked there, she stayed with us, and her boyfriend, I forget his name, and they were also --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object. Mr. President, the questions are asked as to the status of the inhabitants was relevant to the issue as to whether it could have been an UN observation post. In other words, it would not have been an UN observation post if it was used for military purposes. Secondly, it was relevant because of certain other evidence as to the reason for contact with the UN, namely, involving the direct or -- I can't say that any further in the presence of the witness. But I am sure Your Honours recall. This goes well beyond that, well beyond cross-examination. The witness for the second time in a row is embarking on material which is not responsive to the question. In his response to the second last question, indeed he went well beyond the question to a point of, in effect, perhaps contradicting what he said in chief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. What I must say now is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I first ask you something: You asked about the ethnicity of those remaining. The witness has answered that question. I think one of the most relevant aspects of the question might have been whether there were any people remaining in this building, civilians, elderly people living there. Apart from that, the witness also already answered a question about the ethnicity. Would that do in view of what you asked? It is an answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer by "yes or no," Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it would be no, we would be in need of a further explanation, of course. But if it would be yes, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. President, no, this is not sufficient for the following reason: I can be very brief, if you allow me, and we can maybe ask the witness to remove his headphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. For the following reason, Mr. President: We are researching the truth. It is our duty, of all of us, the Prosecution and the Defence. This witness just said that the army was bringing food to these people. And I just found out after the Prosecution asked this witness to come back that the army brought some supplies -- please do not interrupt me -- to the Muslim population. So there is one indispensable element on which we would like to cross-examine since we have here an army who is supporting a Muslim army. And this is quite contrary to an extermination campaign or campaign of terror. This is what I am just discovering at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the army providing food did not -- was not an issue that was raised in cross-examination, but was an answer to a question on living conditions. And it is not an issue that came up during cross-examination, so you may -- the question that you put to the witness has been answered. But you will not be allowed to further explore that area. So please continue with your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gladly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, do you know, since you lived in that area, what was happening when the elderly people died during the war, whatever their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President, for the same reasons as before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, what happened to these people when they died was not an issue that was raised, or did it? I mean, we were talking about who was using the building for what; that was the issue. It was on the basis of the request of the Prosecution, and not on these kind of issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. President. However, the witness himself brought some new elements. He talked about this. He did not say that earlier. Consequently, we are sometimes facing with the obligation to abandon the Anglo-Saxon rigor and to look for the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will allow you one question on this issue, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I will rephrase my question. If you know, tell us, and what can you tell us about the following question: What would happen when people died in that home regardless of their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When some of these people would die in the old people's home, Mrs. Milena had a car Lada and she would put the corpse in that Lada and then she would bury that person in Lasko. That was the name of the cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: This was happening when? During the day? During the night? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I note this is more than one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I allowed you one question, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is sustained. We allowed you one question and the question has been put and answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. President. Since I learned this morning that this witness would be called back, I found in our archives an article. I unfortunately did not have time to have this translated, but I did communicate this document to the Prosecution, who may have had the opportunity to read it. And they also handed out copies to the booth. With your leave, Mr. President, we would like the witness to read a very brief passage of this article which he will be handed, and it concerns precisely a person by the name of Milena. We can see her name on this article. She is the director of this old people's home. And we can see in this article how the old people's home was managed during that period. And since all the documents are handed out to the parties, maybe, with your leave, we could ask the witness to read this very brief passage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I wouldn't know where to start in objecting to that question. First of all, my learned colleague did give us a copy of the article at 2.15 p.m. A minute or two before you walked in. The article is in B/C/S, no English translation, no English summary. And he did not tell us what was in it. Secondly, it does not arise from cross-examination. Thirdly, he has indicated the content without asking the witness to remove his headphones. Fourthly, reading a newspaper article on to the record does not and should not make those words evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. DP6, I see you have taken off the headphones on your own which is very gentle of you. Thank you very much for doing that. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if you -- could you explain further then to the Chamber what is the purpose of these additional questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it seems to me that the Prosecution is really insisting on the fact that this building would have been evacuated at some point or that this building could have been used for some other purposes or whatnot. Very well. But I unfortunately did not have time to have this article translated. First of all, I am not a translator; and secondly, I did not have time to have it done. And we can read in this article what happened during that time. If the witness reads this excerpt, we could see what we are talking about in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I would like you to inform the Chamber what part would you like the witness to read and how it is relevant to the issue you want to raise. Because if you say you could not translate it, I take it that if you ask the witness to read a certain part of it, that you know what is in that part. So would you please first inform the Chamber what is in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it is an article -- it is an interview actually carried out by a reporter, I think it is a newspaper called Vesti the date is the 20th of September, 1994. And it is the issue number 18. A lady, by the name of Milena, it is her first name, this Milena was the director of the old people's home. This article is -- was written before all the procedures, and this article talks about what went on during the war in that old people's home. This is why we have in our hands a document that is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try to cut things short. You want to use this article as evidence that this home was not evacuated, that is how I understand it. Could you tell us what exactly the article says about time. Does it say during the whole conflict? Is there any indication of a precise time to which this -- because it could be highly relevant if it would say, for example, we had difficulties in feeding the elderly in February 1993 and we solved it in this way or whatever. But where can we find a clear indication of time?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we are talking about the war in this article. This article talks about the war. But there are no precise dates covered in this article. They don't say, for instance, something happened in September of 1992 or whatnot. We will not have a chronological -- there is no chronology, there are no dates in this article. We only have the memory of a person relating what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will take a couple of minutes to adjourn and to decide on the issue. --- Break taken at 3.15 p.m

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the Chamber has considered the matter and has decided that this article cannot be put into evidence through this witness unless there would be an opportunity for the Prosecution to examine the source of this information, so that means Milena or whoever it is. Since the Chamber is of the opinion that the witness has testified that there was no evacuation, that is the issue you said you wanted to deal with through this witness and through this article. If that article would support this, then I take it that the Defence takes the view that this would corroborate the evidence of this witness, that there was no evacuation, and then the source of this information, that is, Milena or perhaps also the journalist, should be presented in court. One can wonder whether if you intend to do that, whether it would not be easiest to have it read out by that witness then. But I leave that up to you. So this newspaper article cannot be accepted into evidence unless there is a firm guarantee that the source will be available for cross-examination to the Prosecution. Then the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there would be a specific need by the Defence to have this specific part read out by the witness in respect of the living circumstances - although that was not what you told the Chamber would be the most relevant part - the Chamber does not oppose against having that smaller part read out. Because the Chamber is of the opinion that part of the Prosecution questions also dealt with living circumstances and it might be of interest for the Defence case that living circumstances, but then we are not specifically talking about evacuation. Because if you want to use that article to corroborate the absence of any evacuation, you should call the witness -- you should call the source of this information as a witness. Then the witness may be brought into the courtroom again -- Mr. Ierace, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, just to take a minute in the interest of ultimately saving time. If the Defence had complied with its obligations and given us, told us -- first of all, put to the relevant witnesses that the old people's home was in this position and that the UN had dealings with it, if that would have been put to Mole or Cutler or any one of the others, then I don't think we would have a problem. Secondly, if they told us in advance that this is the evidence they wanted to lead, we could have checked this. It would have been Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. relatively easy for us to check it. And if it was true, I wouldn't be opposing it. In this state, I'm left in a position I've got to test it. Can I just say this, Mr. President, that Senior Military Observer Mole said that there was an observation post in Nedzarici, that that was established by his predecessor, Lieutenant-Colonel Grey, and he, Mole, closed it down. He finished his term in December 1992. His evidence was confirmed by Cutler who replaced Mole. He also said that during Mole's time, the observation post in Nedzarici was closed down. To none of those witnesses was put there was an observation post going on at the very latest of December 1992. I simply make the point if they did it right, we would save a lot of time in court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The situation that now exists, should not have existed, that is for certain. Recalling witnesses should be the exception. We have had earlier occasions where we had to -- where we had to give an opportunity to recall witnesses as well. The Chamber always regrets if there are no good reasons that cause that situation. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, could you tell us, do you insist on, having heard the decision of the Chamber, to have a part read out or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Yes. Because of the short passage that is less than one column of the text, and it also has to do with certain issues regarding the presence of UNPROFOR. It might help to clear the matters up. And I am speaking in the interest of justice, rather than the interest of a sterile confrontation between the parties. Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, for the consideration of the Chamber, that is the first time that you mentioned that the article contains information about the presence of UNPROFOR, isn't it? Wouldn't it have been better to provide this information before the Chamber retired to consider the matter? Would that not have been appropriate? Could you please now -- I would like to turn into closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. DP6, I would like to repeat everything that I said to you at the last occasion where we thought that your examination was concluded. The same thanks from the Tribunal for having come to The Hague, and I am certain that you will be able to return tomorrow. So I would add that the Chamber thanks you for even staying another day where we know that it might not have been easy for you. Thank you very much. We will adjourn until -- no. We will ask the usher now to escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, may I thank the court for their treatment, and I wish my General to arrive at the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. DP6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, I think we have to discuss protective measures for the next witness. So I will like to then turn into closed session unless there is another thing to be raised at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That topic, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will first deal with that and then give an opportunity to Mr. Piletta-Zanin to submit to the court what he intended to submit. Can we --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. What I wish to do pursue the maximum possible equality of arms between the sides. On a number of occasions, the Chamber has requested the Defence to quote this or that passage precisely when it attended to address the matters raised by this or that witness. Yesterday, something out of the ordinary happened. I was examining a witness and I told this witness in the reply to a question put by the Prosecution, you mentioned a mosque. It was objected to. And in his objection the Prosecutor stated publicly that it was not -- that it did not -- in answer to his question that the witness said that. I checked that it was a lie. It was not an error, it was a lie. So, therefore, I should like to ask politely the Prosecution to quote to me the passage where the Prosecution did not ask that question. The Defence, therefore, considers that it is not acceptable that objections be made and that they be said that such-and-such witness has not answered as he did following question by the Prosecution and, therefore, we -- the Defence, loses considerable time in doing this. And then the Chamber once again asks us not to waste time, but we do waste time because we have to -- have to go back to the transcript. We think that this is something that should not be allowed. So the Defence wishes the Rules to be obeyed. We believe that the Prosecution has understood and that the accusations -- the objections increase in number, and the Defence can only repeat that it is not natural whatever the legal system we are talking about, we think it is not acceptable that one side says that it has not said something when it has. We wish to things to be quite clear. We want good cooperation between the parties, then I believe you will have to say -- to say "stop this" we shall not accept. And the Defence indicates this and also indicates that the manner in which a certain episodes certain Boccaccio-esque -- if I may call them that, certain Boccaccio-esque episodes, when they happen, then I think the Chamber should put an end to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I note that I have been accused of lying. The references to yesterday's transcript are at page 14.225, line 14. That is the part of the transcript in which the witness referred to a mosque. The context was, I asked the witness, why did he hold the view that the Institute of Theology effectively was not an important building strategically. He gave a long answer. Part of the answer referred to tall buildings on ABiH territory, and my reading of his answer is that -- and I think it was yours, Mr. President -- was that those tall buildings blocked the view beyond them. I say I think it was yours because you at one point after that said somethings to the positions on the maps that he indicated in that context. In re-examination, Mr. Piletta-Zanin then asked this question which appears at page 14.237, line 5: "Witness, in answer to a question put to you by the Prosecutor, you mentioned that there was a mosque in the neighbourhood of Dobrinja, do you remember this?" "ANSWER: Yes. "QUESTION: Thank you. With regards to that mosque was it ever during the period that we are interested in, was it ever shot at?" In other words, hanging on the word "mosque" in re-examination, my learned colleague sought to open up an entirely different issue. The issue which he raised with the -- I think it was the first witness called by the Defence, whether mosques were deliberately targeted by the SRK. I objected to the question. You asked me whether it went to form or substance, I said substance. And then in support of my objection, I said this commencing at line 17: "Mr. President, it was to the substance of the question." Firstly, the mention of the mosque was not given in response to the question asked by me; secondly, it was not asked in the context of the issue that my friend now seeks to raise for the first time. When I made that objection, I would expect that my words as recorded in the transcript were clearly indicative that the mention by the witness of the word "mosque" was not responsive to the question I asked. I -- suffice to say, I reject the suggestion that I have lied or misled the Trial Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One minute, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, one minute, I mean you have one minute to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, I am sorry. Thank you very much. Mr. President, what we have here is simply that we have to clarify the Rule and to establish the minimum cooperation between the parties. What I am saying is in the full action and Mr. Ierace quoted rightly first [In English] "not given in response to a question asked by me," [Interpretation] that is not true, because it was given within a question. It was part of an answer, that is a fact which cannot be disputed. When that is said then -- you gave me a minute, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you will get the last 30 seconds afterwards. I do understand that there is a disagreement on what these words mean in response of my question. Mr. Ierace interprets this words he used as meaning that the question did not seek that information as a response to that question, whereas Mr. Piletta-Zanin seems to interpret these words as whatever is in an answer, whether that information is sought in the question or not, is in response of that question. So before you continue, I would like to tell the parties that both the interpretations might have their own validity. Please use your last 30 seconds, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should be happy to do this, Mr. President. Only this, when I say that it was in reply, in response, to questions of the Prosecution, then the context is quite clear. It is not a matter whether this was the answer which the Prosecution pursued. But my intervention was it -- if the contents are clear, and where I want to avoid any semantic problems. It wasn't of one's own, well this should not happen again. This is a waste of time; we are wasting time. And we don't like to find some way of mitigating the facts of this as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, given the seriousness of the allegation, could I just say this, that if it was not as I have said, then the second part of my objection does not make sense. I referred specifically to the context in which the word "mosque" was expressed by the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think the issue has been dealt with at this moment at a sufficient level. We will adjourn until a quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, should we turn into closed session in order to hear additional information that you indicated before?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will then turn into closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Perhaps we should stay in the closed session because we shall be asking the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will first ask the witness to make the solemn declaration. I would rather do that in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, my apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. DP10, would you please stand. Before giving testimony in this court, Mr. DP10, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Would you please make that declaration. The text will be handed out to you now by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will then turn into closed session again for your first questions. You will first be examined by counsel for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in open session. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, first I will ask you some questions about you -- about what you knew on that side of the front, what you knew about the scale of destruction. Do you know anything about this -- and I have in mind the material damage, the destruction of buildings -- what can you tell the Chamber about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The destruction took place along the separation lines. I have already said that it was an urban area. Serb soldiers made the trenches inside the buildings, that is, in the entrances of the buildings. And since the Muslims -- since there were trenches, those areas were fired at, and those buildings which were hit directly, destroyed, and demolished by their direct fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. I have to remind you, because all this has to be interpreted, to slow down a little bit, Witness. You tell us that the Muslim side also dug trenches. Did you see those trenches with your own eyes or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course we saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. If you can answer with yes or no, I shall be grateful. Did you see people working there, that is, digging those trenches?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. And insofar as you could see people dig those trenches, do you know who it was, that is, I do not mean individuals, but what was their status, generally speaking? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We never opened fire on those people who were digging those trenches, because we assumed that they were people of Serb ethnicity, so that fire was never opened on those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: These people who were digging, you tell us that they were -- the transcript shows that they were persons who belonged to the Serb culture. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. The witness made an assumption, and the Defence counsel has now mischaracterised that testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, Mr. President, but I haven't finished my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me first wait one second. Up until now, the witness in his answer assumed something. And in the first part of your question, you put it to him as -- not as an assumption, but as a fact. Would you please rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, you told us in your answer that you thought that those persons belonged to the Serb culture. These persons that you talked to us about, that you talk about, what did they look to you as, I am speaking in general terms. What status did they have during the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were people who had remained loyal to the other side. We also had work platoons, as they did. So they were in work platoons, and it was their obligation to do what they were doing as members of a labour platoons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You are talking about labour obligation which came upon them. Can you tell us why.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were out of labour obligation because it was wartime and they were not issued with weapons to go into trenches, possibly because they were Serbs. But Serbs do not just loiter around their houses, I suppose, they sent them to trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You tell us that fire was not opened on those individuals and those people. Did these people wear clothes which made them identifiable?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You could identify them, you could recognise them, because they did not wear BH uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, did you and your unit -- and I am referring to the whole period of war at whatever time -- did you receive any specific instructions relating to civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The instructions of my superiors were never to open fire on civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell us what, at the time, you understood by the word "civilian."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my mind and to my troops, a civilian was every person without a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. These instructions, could you tell us how were they conveyed to you and do you know from which unit, from which structure, were they sent down to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the Serb army, we had the chain of command. I was at the lowest level because I was a platoon commander. I had my company commander who was an officer a lieutenant, Miodrag Djuric was his name. Then there was the battalion commander --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sorry, Witness. Mr. President, I do not know whether the witness should give those names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is not necessary, but if he gives them, unless there are specific reasons to have them redacted, we will just leave them in the transcript. So if there is any specific reason, please tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I do not know. And I am asking. I don't know what is the case and whether perhaps by the fact of ricochet, some certain things might be disclosed. Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you are answering questions, you do not have to give specific names -- of course, you are entitled to do so, and if there is a specific interest to know the name of the persons who you are talking about, then certainly the counsel will ask you to provide these names. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, sorry about interrupting you. Will you please proceed with the answer that you were giving us. You were talking about your chain of command. Will you please finish your sentence.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well then, my company commander was a lieutenant -- I will give you the ranks. So he was a lieutenant, a company commander. The battalion commander was captain 1st class, and the brigade commander was a colonel. And that was my chain, my links of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, these instructions about not targeting civilians, were they communicated to you in writing, for instance, or orally? I don't know. I mean, how were they communicated to you and how frequently?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my -- the practice in my unit was for us, the platoon commanders who were on the front line would have a meeting with the company commander, who would then transmit to us what to do the next day. Of course, in case of an attack against our positions, we had telephone communication and we had code names. For instance, I was a Soka, my command was Jastreb. And then I say, Hello, Jastreb, this is Soka. I am being attacked from such-and-such sight, what am I to do? And then my lieutenants would issue me these -- would give me the instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. How many times, if you know that -- and of course I am asking about an order of magnitude. But, of course, your chain of command, how often did your chain of command remind you of this instruction, not to target individuals or to do one's utmost not to target -- not to hit individuals -- civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I was clear. We had our meetings every night, and every night we would be given these instructions. And every night we would be told not to target civilians and not to target without any need or not to target without any need because we had to -- we were rather short on ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. But -- yes, you have already answered a part of my question because I wanted to ask you about the ammunition. Did you receive any specific instructions concerning the use of ammunition, that is, specifically the quantity, the quota, if you like, that would be allotted to this or that unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since this urban area, as I call it, is linked with this site, with our logistics, but one street only, Bana Sur Bata Street. And in 1992, 1993, it was impossible to move about and bring ammunition in. So that was the reason. And besides, by George, there wasn't enough ammunition. That was the early days. When we got to the barracks, some people fired off just like that. So that later on we were issued with only as much ammunition as our commanders believed we would need for our defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: With regards to the use of this ammunition, which were the instructions which you received? And this stems from your previous answer, but I will rephrase it and put it to you. Did you receive any instructions with regards to the quantities with regards to the use and the usage of this ammunition?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, there were. With regards to ordinary ammunition and ordinary ammunition we call rifle ammunition. And afterwards, when I was a member of the battalion, we were talking about heavy ammunition, that we never had enough. And we had to be careful and to save it just in case we had to defend ourselves. We had to make sure that we always have enough -- enough ammunition to defend ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for these answers. Witness do you have any direct experience with regards to weaponry, and I am especially referring to artillery weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the witness speak more slowly, please, or slower. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, could you please just slow down. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my previous answer I refer to the fact that in my unit, my company had the largest calibre -- the ammunition that had the largest calibre was 20 millimetres. That was the largest and most lethalest of ammunitions that my unit possessed. With regards to all the other ammunition, it was ammunition for rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. But my question was to the effect to find out if you yourself had the occasion to be present during some shellings on the zone that you were defending, or were you present in the neighbourhoods corresponding to the responsibility area of your own company? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had almost daily shellings. One of my soldiers --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't seize what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One day, he was a transport in an APC with an open roof. And that soldier was hit directly on the head. It was a tragic accident.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: He was hit on the head by what? What type of projectile?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: What kind of shell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of which calibre, but it was a shell and it hit the roof of the vehicle. And I believe that the width of this roof was 70 centimetres, but I couldn't tell you which calibre hit him. It just really exploded.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Since you are in your own language saying "Granata" and that this word in the Serbian language encompasses a few things. It can also mean mortar. I would like to ask you the following questions: What was the weapon that launched this grenade or this shell? I don't necessarily mean which diametre was, which calibre, but what type was it exactly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a mortar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, when you were saying that you were shelled on a daily basis, what kind of artillery fire was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was all mortars, mortar shells [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a slight interpretation problem in the French booth. I am not even sure even if in English that the witness said that it was "only mortar shells." I think he said "mortars, not only mortars," which is a bit different. So I will rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Were there any other types of shells, in other words, any other weapons used other than the mortars that were used on the areas that we are talking of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From shorter distances from one line to the other, you see, we were sometimes as close to 20 metres from the other line. So it -- they were hitting us with Zoljas, Tromblon, hand-held launchers, and what we call infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. In terms of heavy weapons, however, were there any heavy weapons that would have targeted your units during the conflict period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From personal experience, I can tell you that we had a few tanks, and a part of the mechanised armoured battalion, and we also had some tanks at our disposal. We never used those tanks because we never had to shoot on the city or use them for the city. But one of the tanks were not functioning very well, so we had to remove it from Grbavica on to Lukavica in order to remove it from there. And in the street Bana Sur Bata, the tank was hit. And the hit came from whom? This is what we were able to assess. It was a 55 tank shell and the driver who was inside was killed. This is all I can tell us of my personal experience and I was a witness of this event.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, you were telling us that you were present during this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And for the French booth, that was going towards Lukavica, and not towards Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: How can you tell that the shot came from a tank, that it was a tank shot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are talking about an APC, and so the thickness of the material in which it was built is 20 to 30 millimetre. And this shell went right through and we found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I would like to talk about the distance between the lines during the conflict. What was, Witness, if you know it, not the length of the line that you were holding but what was the depth towards the back? And I am thinking about this whole technical area, the depth of your line. Can you tell us what it was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: With regards to Grbavica from Sarajevo, Grbavica to Sarajevo is separated by the Miljacka River. Our lines were on one side of the Miljacka River, the Muslin army was on the other side of the Miljacka River. With regards to the interior, the inside of Grbavica, Grbavica is an area where you had civilians who lived there. So there is no depth, if you will. From our line to the place where civilians lived, there is not even more than 1.500 to 2.000 metres. So from the river Miljacka to street Moravska which belongs to the city. Actually 1500 metres away from there, there was the civilian population, but they were not only Serbs, there was also a Muslim portion, the Muslim --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, perhaps I missed it, but do we know already what confrontation lines we are talking about precisely? I mean, it has been of -- it seems to be of major importance for the Defence case, and we have details. Is this general information for all the front lines, or is this the part where the witness was stationed or --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in fact, in French, I was asking him "the lines" what were the lines that this person had the knowledge of. He knew two lines because he witnessed these two situations, from the beginning -- actually he began working there in October of 1992. The witness answers about Grbavica. It is his second position. I was asking -- actually I was waiting for the end of his answer in order to ask him a question with regards to the first situation, the first position. We will show the witness later some maps after the break, and the witness will be able to show us precisely the positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is mainly in respect of the earlier answers that I had some difficulties in following where we were exactly talking about. Would this be a suitable moment for a break or would you have --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just two more questions and then we will be able to go and have a break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, very briefly, you told us what the situation was like in Grbavica. But can you tell us: What was the situation for the first line? What was it like -- what was the technical depth on the first line that you knew, that you were at? Can you tell us what it was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not understand -- you are talking about the depth of the line that was held by the Serbian army? Is that what you asking me? Is that the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I am talking to you about the lines that you yourself have defended as a soldier and the positions that you -- you personally -- and I am not talking about the length of the line, all the technical zone, all the technical area that you have in the back. The logistic area, the commandment area. So for you, what was that depth? If you know it, of course.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said earlier that from the line where the Serbian soldier was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. standing, behind him there were people who lived on the Serbian side and there was from 1500 metres to 2 kilometres, that's all. We didn't have any other depth.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I just add, when I am talking about the line, I mean to say that behind us was of Serbian responsibility, but the area from which we were able to look towards the city and the position where you could die was not over 2.000 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. At the very beginning of your testimony, you mentioned there were some destruction that took place on the line. Do you include in your answer the zone of a kilometre or 1.5 kilometres when you talked about the destruction behind you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP6 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the line was such, and behind us we had these buildings, and these buildings were completely destroyed by Tromblons, Zoljas, hand-held launchers. But with regards to the area where civilians lived, they were shelled, so mortars did their damage. And this is how they were able to destroy the part where civilians lived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, it still is entirely unclear. May I ask you one or two questions: When you were at the front line or confrontation lines, did you stay at the same position during the whole armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. President, could the witness speak slower.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The task of my unit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am just asking whether you were moving or whether you stayed at the same position.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was your unit moving during the war or were you stationed at different positions for a certain period of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were always in Grbavica, which doesn't mean that it was always at the same post, the same spot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were at positions in Grbavica for the entire period of the armed conflict? That's clear. Thank you for this answer. We will then adjourn until -- Mr. Ierace, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, at some stage, perhaps at the beginning of the next session, could I take a few minutes to deal with a matter in relation to forthcoming witnesses and exhibits, giving that this is the last hearing day before Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time would you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It would only take me a minute to say what I have to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could we not do this at the very end of today's session? We will continue with the witness. And it seems to be more logical that we just pursue what we started with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We do not know yet what Mr. Ierace wants to tell us. So I would prefer, as a matter of fact, if it takes only one minute to ask the witness to leave the courtroom and to do it right now. So that if it needs some thinking, that we can do that during the break. Mr. Usher, may I ask you to escort the witness out of the courtroom. We will have a break for approximately 20 minutes, 25 minutes, Mr. DP10.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if I may. If some questions are put to you, I will not be able to answer by myself. Usually my colleague deals with lots of issues, and she is not present today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I take it that the Defence present at the hearing should be in a position to answer the questions. I mean, that is the -- if lead counsel is not there, those who are there in her place should be able to answer questions. But of course, if there is any specific issue, we will see how important it is. Mr. Ierace, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Yesterday we received from the Registry a photocopy of a letter that the Registry had received addressed to me from the Defence dated the 20th of October. But having regard to the fax information, it seems it was faxed to the Registry on the 22nd of October. The letter sets out the order of witnesses for the week from the 28th of October to the 1st of November. It makes no mention of the witnesses to be called next week. Firstly, might I respectfully suggest, that in future, the Defence provides running commentaries, in other words, a running list, who are the witnesses to be called from the next witness. So, therefore, could the Defence confirm that the next witness after this one -- and perhaps I should indicate that list in closed session. But essentially, at some stage, could the Defence confirm the identity of the witnesses to be called next week and the order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you try to find out during the next break whether you agree on that or not. And if not, we will then deal with it in closed session --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And secondly, Mr. President, the letter we received from the Registry says that a description of the provisional exhibits is attached. As I understand it, the Registry only received one page, no attachment. Finally, it refers -- the letter refers to a number of exhibits in the form of SRK documents to be tendered. There is no indication as to through which witnesses the documents will be tendered, and therefore no indication as to when they will be tendered. So perhaps my learned colleague can attend to those matters. Thank you. And perhaps during the break he can give me the list of witnesses for next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I take it, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you could provide Mr. Ierace with the calling order of the witnesses for next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My answer is no, Mr. President, for the simple reason that I do not have these documents here at hand. Secondly, I do not remember it by heart, and thirdly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please deal with the matter during the break as well, and I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gladly --
